text: Which version is correct? 'Each of the students ___ submitted the assignment.'
options: Each of the students has submitted the assignment.|Each of the students have submitted the assignment.|Each of the student have submitted the assignment.|Each of the student has submitted the assignment.
explanation: 'Each' is singular, so the verb is 'has', and 'of the' is followed by the plural 'students'. Each of the students has submitted the assignment. The commonest error is letting the nearby plural pull the verb into 'have'.

text: Which version is correct? 'She is better ___ mathematics ___ I am.'
options: She is better at mathematics than I am.|She is better in mathematics than me.|She is more better at mathematics than me.|She is better at mathematics then I am.
explanation: One is good AT a subject, the comparison takes 'than I am' rather than 'than me' when a verb follows, 'more better' doubles the comparative, and 'then' is about time while 'than' makes comparisons. She is better at mathematics than I am.

text: Which version is correct? 'Neither the students ___ the lecturer ___ present.'
options: Neither the students nor the lecturer was present.|Neither the students nor the lecturer were present.|Neither the students or the lecturer was present.|Neither of the students nor the lecturer were present.
explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, which here is the singular 'lecturer': was present. 'Neither ... or' is not a pair, and 'neither of' takes two things rather than a list. Neither the students nor the lecturer was present.

text: Which version is correct, and attaches the opening phrase to the person who finished the paper?
options: Having finished the paper, she left the hall.|Having finished the paper, the hall was left by her.|Finishing the paper, the hall was left.|Having finished the paper, the hall emptied.
explanation: The opening phrase describes whoever finished the paper, so the subject that follows must be that person. Having finished the paper, she left the hall. The other three attach the phrase to the hall, which did not finish anything -- a dangling modifier.

text: Which version is correct? '___ of applications ___ risen sharply.'
options: The number of applications has risen sharply.|The number of applications have risen sharply.|A number of applications has risen sharply.|The numbers of application has risen sharply.
explanation: 'The number' is a singular thing and takes 'has'; 'a number of' means 'several' and would take 'have'. The number of applications has risen sharply.

text: Which version reports correctly what he said about Friday?
options: He said that he would submit the report by Friday.|He said that he will submit the report by Friday.|He said that he would submitted the report by Friday.|He says that he would submit the report by Friday.
explanation: A past reporting verb ('said') moves 'will' to 'would' and keeps the plain infinitive 'submit'. He said that he would submit the report by Friday.

text: Which version is correct in a hypothetical about revision?
options: If I were you, I would revise the weaker topics first.|If I was you, I would revise the weaker topics first.|If I were you, I will revise the weaker topics first.|If I am you, I would revise the weaker topics first.
explanation: A hypothetical takes the subjunctive 'were' and pairs it with 'would'. If I were you, I would revise the weaker topics first. 'Was' is the plain past and 'will' breaks the pairing.

text: Which version is correct about a committee and a deadline?
options: The committee is divided on whether to extend the deadline.|The committee are divided on whether to extend the deadline.|The committee is divided on if to extend the deadline.|The committee is divided whether to extend the deadline.
explanation: In Indian and British usage a committee acting as one body takes a singular verb; 'whether' rather than 'if' introduces a choice before an infinitive; and 'divided on' needs its preposition. The committee is divided on whether to extend the deadline.

text: Which version is correct about how long she has worked here?
options: She has been working here since 2021.|She is working here since 2021.|She works here since 2021.|She has been working here from 2021.
explanation: An action continuing from a point in the past takes the present perfect continuous with 'since' for that point. She has been working here since 2021. The present tense cannot carry 'since', and 'from' needs an end point to pair with.

text: Which version is correct about the bell and the students leaving?
options: Hardly had the bell rung when the students left the hall.|Hardly the bell had rung when the students left the hall.|Hardly had the bell rung than the students left the hall.|Hardly had the bell rang when the students left the hall.
explanation: 'Hardly' at the front inverts the auxiliary ('had the bell rung'), pairs with 'when', and takes the past participle 'rung'. Hardly had the bell rung when the students left the hall. 'Than' pairs with 'no sooner', not with 'hardly'.

text: Find the part with the error: (A) The list of selected candidates / (B) have been put up / (C) on the notice board. / (D) No error
explanation: The subject is 'the list', which is singular, so it should be 'has been put up'. The error is in part B. The plural 'candidates' sitting next to the verb is what makes the mistake feel right.

text: Find the part with the error: (A) She is one of the / (B) most brilliant student / (C) in the department. / (D) No error
explanation: 'One of the' is followed by a plural: 'most brilliant students'. The error is in part B.

text: Find the part with the error: (A) Although he worked hard, / (B) but he could not / (C) clear the cutoff. / (D) No error
explanation: 'Although' already joins the two clauses, so the 'but' in part B is one conjunction too many. The error is in part B -- use either 'Although he worked hard, he could not' or 'He worked hard, but he could not'.

text: Find the part with the error: (A) The teacher asked the students / (B) that why they had not / (C) submitted the assignment. / (D) No error
explanation: Reported questions take the question word alone, not 'that' before it: 'why they had not'. The error is in part B.

text: Find the part with the error: (A) Each of the four sections / (B) carry a separate cutoff / (C) in this pattern. / (D) No error
explanation: 'Each' is singular, so the verb is 'carries'. The error is in part B.

text: Find the part with the error: (A) Neither of the two candidates / (B) were able to answer / (C) the last question. / (D) No error
explanation: 'Neither of' two things is singular, so it is 'was able to answer'. The error is in part B.

text: Choose the word closest in meaning to ABUNDANT.
explanation: Abundant means existing in large quantity, so plentiful is closest. Scarce is its opposite, and the other two describe different properties altogether.

text: Choose the word closest in meaning to CANDID.
explanation: Candid means open and straightforward in speech, so frank is closest. Secretive is the opposite; cheerful and careless describe other things entirely.

text: Choose the word closest in meaning to METICULOUS.
explanation: Meticulous means showing great attention to detail, so careful is closest. Hasty is its opposite in practice, and the other two are unrelated qualities.

text: Choose the word closest in meaning to CONCISE.
explanation: Concise means saying much in few words, so brief is closest. 'Complete' is the tempting wrong answer: a concise account can be complete, but the word is about length and not about coverage.

text: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to TRANSPARENT.
explanation: Transparent lets light through, so its opposite is opaque. 'Visible' is close to transparent in sense rather than opposed to it, which is what makes it the distractor.

text: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to DILIGENT.
explanation: Diligent means hard-working and careful, so lazy is its opposite. The other three are qualities a diligent person may or may not have, which is not the same as being opposed.

text: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to AMPLIFY.
explanation: To amplify is to make larger or louder, so to reduce is its opposite. 'Explain' catches a second sense of amplify -- to add detail -- but even there the opposite would be to abbreviate, not to explain.

text: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to TENTATIVE.
explanation: Tentative means not yet settled, so definite is its opposite. 'Temporary' is the trap: a tentative plan is unsettled, while a temporary one is settled but short-lived.
